To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the evolution of morphologically complex organisms is shaped by paleopolyploidization and retention of transcriptional regulators, and that these regulators are major driving forces for the evolution of morphologic complexity.

1) The number of transcriptional regulators (TAPs) per genome is a strong predictor of morphological complexity in Viridiplantea, 2) The number of TAP per genome is significantly correlated with paleopolyploidization and 3) TAPs have been lost and gained throughout Viridiplantaea evolution, with major bursts of gain and expansion occurring in the water-to- land transition and the radiation flowering plants.

the gain and expansion of transcription-associated proteins (i.e. transcription factors and other regulators) is a major driving force behind the evolution of plant morphological complexity and that this gain and expansion has been shaped significantly by the paleopolyploidization events that occurred during the radiation of flowering plant lineages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the number and type of transcription factors and other regulatory genes have changed during the evolution of the plant kingdom.
the question how the evolution of gene regulation has been shaping the morphological evolution of plants, especially the evolution of morphogenetic complexity.
the evolution of the regulatory networks of plants and algae and the evolution of morpho-physiological complexity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the number of TAPS per genome is a good proxy for organismal complexity and is shaped by polyploidizations.
the evolution of morpho-anatomical complexity in plants is driven by the gain and expansion of TAPs, and this expansion is significantly correlated to polyploidization.
plant morphological complexity is significantly shaped by polyploidizations and subsequent biased paleo-log retention of TAPs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the evolution of morphologic complexity in plants has been shaped by two major bursts of TAP gain and/or expansion, the first coinciding with the transition from water to land and the second with the radiation of flowering plant lineages.
TAPs and their regulatory networks are major driving forces in the evolution of morphologic complexity, especially within plants.

, in Plantae, the evolution of morpho-anatomical complexity has been driven by polyploidizations, which have been followed by the biased retention of paleologs encoding TAPs, which in turn have been responsible for the evolution of the morpho-anatomies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of morphologic complexity in plants is shaped by polyploidizations and the retention of duplicated transcriptional regulators.

the evolution of morphologic complexity in plants is shaped significantly by poliploidization, which is accompanied by a biased retention of duplicated transcription-associated genes, especially transcription factors.
TAPs have played an important role in the evolution of morphologic complexity in Plantae.
